qa.question:
During the year, the group launched several residential projects in Singapore, including 
River Modern (100% interest), Springleaf Residence (60%), Faber Residence (50%), Penrith 
(30%) and Tengah Garden Residences (20%).  
 
All of these projects recorded strong take-up during their respective launch weekends and 
are now all more than 90% sold within the first 12 months of sales. The group’s share of 
unrecognised sales value from units already sold exceeded $3 billion as at 30 June 2026. As 
most of these projects are still at an early stage of construction, the majority of the associated 
revenue has yet to be recognised despite the projects being substantially sold.  
 
Looking ahead, the group has an upcoming project at Lentor Hills estate, in which it holds a 
50% interest, targeted for launch in the first half of 2027, as well as the Berlayar Drive 
project, in which it holds a 40% interest.  
 
Information on the group’s residential projects in Singapore is set out on page 160 of the 
annual report.  
 
(i) 
Does the group have any formal or informal strategic arrangement with 
Hong Leong Holdings Limited (HLHL) in relation to residential development 
projects? How does management determine whether to undertake a project 
independently, as with River Modern, or jointly with HLHL or other 
partners? 
 
(ii) 
What are the key factors that determine the group’s ownership interest in 
joint venture projects, particularly where its stake has ranged from 20% to 
60% for recent projects? 
 
(iii) 
For its joint venture projects, how are major decisions made between the 
group and its partner(s), particularly on land acquisition strategy 
(including bids), development strategy, pricing, and sales? 
 
In August 2026, the group, along with HLHL, was the successful bidder for the Berlayar Drive 
residential site at $1,515 per square foot per plot ratio. This site has a relatively low plot 
ratio of 1.4, a five-storey height limit and attracted only one bid in the tender. 
 
Based on reported market analysis, this was the highest land rate achieved for a pure 
residential Government Land Sale site in the Rest of Central Region and was 14% higher than 
the land cost for the maiden Berlayar estate site tendered in November 2025.  
 
(iv) 
Given the Berlayar Drive site’s low plot ratio, five-storey height limit and 
relatively high land cost, how does management see the optimal 
development strategy for the site? What is different about the risk and 
return profile compared with the group’s recent higher-density projects, 
and what gives management confidence that the project can generate an 
appropriate return on the $1,515 psf ppr land cost?

The group successfully privatised GuocoLand (Malaysia) Berhad (GLM) through a 
selective capital reduction and repayment exercise at RM1.10 per share, with GLM 
subsequently delisted from Bursa Malaysia Securities Berhad on 18 August 2026. 
 
An independent assessment valued GLM’s revalued net asset value at RM2.96 per share. 
Management has stated that, following the privatisation, it intends to further streamline 
operations, unlock latent value where appropriate and identify a new direction for the 
Malaysia business. 
 
(i) 
How is the strategic review of the Malaysia business being conducted, and 
who is leading the process? What specific objectives and criteria has the 
board given management for assessing the businesses, assets and capital 
currently deployed in Malaysia? 
 
(ii) 
What is the expected timeline for completing the strategic review and 
communicating the group’s new direction for Malaysia? 
 
(iii) 
Is the board also evaluating the group’s strategic options for Tower Real 
Estate Investment Trust?  
 
Separately, Note 31 disclosed that GLM disposed of a 20% equity interest in GLM REIT 
Management Sdn Bhd to a related company, HL Management Co Sdn Bhd, a wholly-owned 
subsidiary of Hong Leong Company (Malaysia) Bhd. 
 
(iv) 
What was the strategic rationale behind this disposal in the REIT manager? 
Was this considered an interested person transaction under SGX listing 
rules, and how was the consideration determined?

The company has an in-house internal audit function led by the Group Head of Internal 
Audit, Mr Jason Ho, and supported by other team members. The internal audit function 
operates in accordance with the Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing 
issued by The Institute of Internal Auditors. 
 
(i) 
Can the audit and risk committee (ARC) provide greater visibility on the size 
and capabilities of the internal audit function, including the number of team 
members, their relevant experience and qualifications, and how the ARC 
assesses whether the function is adequately resourced for the group’s size 
and risk profile? 
 
(ii) 
What was the scope of the internal audit in FY2026? What were the key 
findings? 
 
It would appear that the Group Head of Internal Audit has been in the role for more than 10 
years.  

(iii) 
Has the ARC considered whether periodic rotation of the internal audit 
leadership, or an independent assessment of the function’s effectiveness 
and objectivity, would be appropriate? How does the ARC satisfy itself that 
the internal audit function remains sufficiently independent and objective 
after a long tenure?

qa.question:
As at 30 June 2026, the group’s network includes 12 general practitioner (GP) clinics, 5 
specialist centres and 1 allied health services clinic providing traditional Chinese medicine 
(TCM) services. The group has decided to cease its TCM business following the landlord’s 
notice to surrender the premises for redevelopment. The group has also ceased its 
physiotherapy operations since May 2025, while its dermatology and laser specialist clinic 
entered liquidation proceedings in February 2026. 
 
(Source: company annual report) 
 
(i) 
With the exit from these businesses, how does the board reassess the 
viability of the group’s healthcare ecosystem with only two remaining 
segments? To what extent does the exit from these businesses affect the 
synergies within the group’s healthcare ecosystem, and what is the board’s 
revised strategic direction for the remaining businesses? 
 
The group recorded a loss attributable to owners of $0.86 million in FY2026, following a loss 
of $4.03 million in FY2025. 
 
(ii) 
Other than PTL Spine & Orthopaedics Private Limited, can management 
identify which clinics, if any, are loss-making? What specific operational 
step is management taking to achieve sustainable profitability across its GP 
and specialist clinics? What specific measures are being taken to improve 
clinic-level economics, and can management quantify the expected 
contribution from each key lever, including pricing, utilisation, staff costs, 
rental and overhead rationalisation? 

As at 30 June 2026, the group’s goodwill amounted to approximately $10.3 million, 
representing 33% of the group’s total assets. Over the years, the group recognised 
impairment losses on goodwill of PTL Spine & Orthopaedics Private Limited in FY2025 and 
FY2026 amounting to its entire goodwill of $3.12 million and $644,000 from AE Medical 
Sengkang Pte. Ltd. in FY2025.  
 
The group has also recognised impairment losses on investments in associates, including 
approximately $0.29 million in FY2026 relating to KCS Anaesthesia Services Pte. Ltd., $0.29 
million in FY2025 relating to Shanghai Gong Pu Sheng Jia Medical Management Center, and 
$0.73 million and $1.11 million in FY2024 and FY2023, respectively, relating to Sen Medical 
Holdings. 
 
(iii) 
Given these impairment charges, what changes have the directors made to 
the group’s acquisition criteria, valuation discipline and post-acquisition 
oversight to prevent further destruction of shareholder value? 
 
In addition, in February 2026, the company acquired a 51% equity interest in TS Medical 
Pte. Ltd. for $578,000 in cash. Under the agreement, the vendor provided revenue 
guarantees1 for specified periods, with potential compensation payable if certain agreed 
revenue targets are not achieved. 
 
(iv) 
How did the board assess whether the revenue guarantee is consistent with 
the applicable ethics requirements established by Singapore Medical 
Council? In particular, how is the arrangement structured to ensure that the 
revenue guarantees, and the compensation mechanism, do not create 
pressure on doctors to make clinical decisions based on financial 
considerations? What effective safeguards are in place to monitor 
compliance and ensure that clinical decisions remain independent of 
financial considerations?

In May 2026, PuXiang Healthcare Holdings Limited submitted an application for a 
potential listing on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. If successful, the listing could provide a 
liquidity opportunity and a potential valuation benchmark for the group's investment. 
 
 
1 In April 2017, the Singapore Medical Association iterated that ethical guidelines for the medical 
profession prohibit profit guarantees involving healthcare services as the financial imperative they 
impose is incompatible with the guidelines. Specifically, to avoid situations where a doctor’s 
professional judgment is, or is seen to be, influenced by financial considerations, Section H3.1(c) of 
the 2016 Singapore Medical Council’s “Handbook on Medical Ethics” states that a doctor ought to be 
careful to: 
 
“Not to allow any financial arrangement that commits you to give a revenue or profit guarantee to 
a third party to influence how you manage patients. You should avoid such arrangements as a 
matter of good practice as the pressures on you to meet your financial obligations would be great”. 

Through its 51%-owned joint venture, Singapore Paincare Capital Pte. Ltd., the group holds 
2,777,778 Series A+ preference shares in PuXiang, acquired at RMB14.40 per share for a total 
cost of approximately RMB40 million. The preference shares are convertible into a 2.42% 
equity interest in PuXiang. 
 
(i) 
What is management’s role in the IPO, if any? If PuXiang successfully lists on 
the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, what is the group's intended strategy for its 
investment, including whether it plans to retain or monetise the stake? 
 
(ii) 
Will the group be permitted to sell any of its shares as part of the IPO, subject 
to the applicable listing requirements and any lock-up restrictions? If not, 
what are the expected restrictions and potential timeline for realising value 
from the investment? 
 
The operations of the group's China associates, Beijing Puxin and Shanghai Gong Pu Sheng 
Jia Medical Management Center, are currently on hold while their controlling shareholders 
reassess their long-term plans and focus on the proposed PuXiang listing. 
 
(iii) 
To what extent can the group protect its investment and influence decisions 
on restarting operations, additional funding or an eventual exit? What 
contractual or governance rights does the group have to influence 
operational and strategic decisions, and to what extent is it dependent on 
its Chinese partners?

qa.question:
Revenue from the Distribution and Services Solutions (DSS) segment increased by 23% 
in FY2026, benefitting from strong growth in the global semiconductor market. Singapore 
and China remain the segment’s key markets, with segment revenue of $71.0 million and 
operating profit of $4.0 million. 
 
The group will pursue new business opportunities in Southeast Asia, Taiwan and India, while 
expanding its product and service offerings to capture the growth of the buoyant market. 
 
Singapore revenue increased by approximately one-third, while China revenue declined by 
approximately 14%.  
 
(i) 
Can management explain the key factors behind this divergence? In 
particular, how much of the growth in Singapore was driven by underlying 
volume and customer wins, as opposed to market or product mix, and what 
is management’s outlook for the China business??  
 
(ii) 
How much of the group’s revenue could be attributed to underlying demand 
for artificial intelligence (AI)? How does management distinguish the 
current AI-driven demand from the normal semiconductor cycle? What 
indicators does management monitor to determine whether current 
demand is structural or cyclical, and what would be the potential impact on 
the DSS business if AI-related semiconductor demand were to moderate 
materially? 
 
(iii) 
Across Southeast Asia, Taiwan and India, what are the specific growth 
opportunities that management believes can materially expand the DSS 
business over the next three to five years?  
 
Despite the reported accounting profit, the group reported net cash used in operating 
activities of $2.9 million. This was mainly due to a significant increase in trade and other 
receivables of $7.2 million, offset by $4.2 million increase in trade and other payables (page 
114; Consolidated statement of cash flows).  
 
(iv) 
Can management explain the underlying reasons for the increase in 
receivables and confirm how much had been collected after the reporting 
date? What is the group’s normal cash conversion cycle for the DSS 
business?

Would the board and management provide shareholders with greater clarity on the 
group’s other businesses and how these investments are expected to contribute to long-term 
shareholder value? 
 
(i) 
Egg production and distribution: On 29 September 2026, the Group announced 
the groundbreaking for the egg farm under ISE Foods Holdings Pte. Ltd., in which 
the group now holds a 43% interest following the entry of Unicore Agri Pte. Ltd. 
as a co-investor. The first phase is expected to take less than two years to 
complete, with eggs from the smart farms expected to reach the market in 2028. 
The initial phase will comprise nine layer houses and three pullet houses, with 
capacity for 1.35 million layers and 450,000 pullets and annual production of 
approximately 380 million eggs. What is the group’s expected level of 
management involvement during the construction and ramp-up phases? A 
term loan facility of up to $65 million has been secured to partially finance the 
development. Is this financing on a recourse or non-recourse basis, and to 
what extent is the group directly or indirectly exposed to the debt, including 
through guarantees, security or other support? 
 
(ii) 
Indoor golf simulator (GreenBox by My Golf Kaki): The group introduced its 
golf simulator business, with two centres now operating at Orchid Country Club 
and Downtown East in collaboration with Uplay Ventures Pte. Ltd., an affiliate of 
NTUC Club. What is the business model for GreenBox, including its target 
customers, revenue drivers and key operating costs, and what level of 
revenue or utilisation is required to reach breakeven? Segment loss 
increased from $771,000 in FY2025 to $1.68 million in FY2026. What does 
management believe is the business’s sustainable competitive advantage 
and why does the group believe it can build a viable business in this area? 
How much capital has the board committed or capped for GreenBox?   
 
(iii) 
Bintan: In the letter to shareholders, the group stated that feasibility studies 
would be conducted to determine the long-term strategy for the Bintan asset. 
After more than seven years of ownership, what has the board established 
about the commercial potential and optimal use of the land to date? What 
are the key questions that the feasibility studies are intended to resolve, and 
when does the board expect to reach a firm decision on the asset’s 

development or monetisation strategy? If strategic direction and execution 
are principally being driven by the 25% minority shareholder, how does the 
board satisfy itself that the group has sufficient influence, information and 
ability to challenge the strategy?

qa.question:
For FY2026, the group recorded revenue of $617.4 million, compared with $230.2 
million in the previous year, with the increase primarily driven by progressive revenue 
recognition from River Green and The LakeGarden Residences. River Green in River Valley 
has achieved approximately 95% take-up, while The LakeGarden Residences in the Jurong 
Lake District is more than 99% sold.  
 
The group has also secured, together with Metro Holdings, a 99-year leasehold residential 
site at Dunearn Road under the Government Land Sales programme. The site, located within 
the upcoming Bukit Timah Turf City precinct, is planned for approximately 330 residential 
units. The joint venture submitted the top bid of $533 million, or $1,625 psf per plot ratio. 
This is 15% higher than the $1,410 psf ppr land rate for an adjacent plot awarded last year 
to another consortium of developers.  
 
(i) 
What was the strategic rationale for bringing a partner into the Dunearn 
Road project rather than developing the site independently? Beyond 
providing capital, what specific capabilities, risk-sharing or other value 
does the partner bring to the project? More broadly speaking, how does the 
board and management determine the appropriate pace of new residential 
land acquisition and development in Singapore, including when to scale up 
or slow down? 
 
The group also has property interests overseas. In Malaysia, it has acquired a freehold land 
parcel in Mont Kiara, Kuala Lumpur, for a planned premium residential development of 
approximately 266 units. In Australia, planning work is underway for developments at 464 
St Kilda Road and 380 Flinders Street in Melbourne. The group's property business activities 
in Australia are conducted through its investment arm. 
 
(Source: company annual report; emphasis added) 
 
From Note 34, it can be seen that the group’s non-current assets in Australia have exceeded 
those in Malaysia, although its revenue contribution has remained relatively modest over 
the years.  

Planning work for 464 St Kilda Road has been described as ongoing in the annual reports for 
the past three years. 
 
(ii) 
What is the size, bandwidth and leadership depth of the group's Australian 
team, and why are the group’s development activities conducted through 
the investment arm rather than the group's core property development 
business?  
 
(iii) 
Given the capital committed to Australia relative to its current revenue 
contribution, how does management assess the productivity and strategic 
value of the Australian portfolio? 
 
(iv) 
Separately, what specific role does the group play in DRC1 and, through DRC, 
in the management and value creation of its investment in Amara?

On the retail side, the group is expanding its store network and introducing new brands, 
such as Charles Tyrwhitt and JNBY, while Uniqlo continues to demonstrate strong top-line 
growth in both Singapore and Malaysia.  
 
(i) 
Can management explain the strategic rationale and selection criteria for 
introducing new brands into the portfolio? What financial and operating 
criteria does the board apply when approving new brand introductions and 
store openings? For example, what hurdle rates for return on invested 
capital, payback period and store-level profitability are required, and how 
are the underlying assumptions stress-tested prior to approval? 
 
(ii) 
How does the board assess whether G2000 remains relevant and 
competitive in today’s retail environment? What key performance 
indicators does the board track to monitor the brand's health, including 
customer numbers, footfall, transaction volumes, average transaction value 
and same-store sales growth? How does the board use these metrics to 
determine whether strategic or operational changes are required?

In the chairman’s message to shareholders, he highlighted that the group’s net asset 
value per share increased from $3.73 as at 30 June 2025 to $3.92 as at 30 June 2026.  
 
However, the share price has traded between $1.40 and $1.72 over the last year and trades 
around $1.50 even though there has been renewed market interest in the local bourse, 
pushing the STI up to all-time highs in recent weeks.

strategy, capital optimisation and investor engagement. 
 
(i) 
Has the board assessed whether the group could benefit from any of the 
initiatives under the programme, particularly in strengthening its strategy, 
capital allocation and investor engagement? If so, what specific measures is 
the board considering? 
 
Resolution 9 in the Notice of AGM seeks shareholders’ approval for a share purchase 
mandate. The company last repurchased its shares in October 2022.  
 
(ii) 
Given the significant discount between the company’s share price and 
reported NAV, what valuation, liquidity, capital and other criteria would the 
board apply in determining whether share buybacks would be an 
appropriate use of capital? 
 
(iii) 
To what extent does the board consider the discount to NAV to reflect the

Lum Chang Creations Limited (LCC) was listed on the Catalist Board in July 2025 and 
successfully transferred to the Mainboard of the Singapore Exchange on 16 July 2026.  
 
On 18 June 2026, the company divested 12.3 million ordinary shares of LCC at $0.759 per 
share through a placement exercise, generating net proceeds of $9.1 million. In the same 
exercise, Mr Lim Thiam Hooi, the managing director of LCC, also sold 7.7 million shares for

Following the placement, the Group’s effective interest in LCC was diluted from 71.11% to

shareholders, can the board clarify the respective roles and decision-
making responsibilities of the company and LCC? In particular, which 
matters remain subject to oversight or approval by the company, and how 
does the company ensure that LCC’s board can exercise independent 
judgement while the company continues to be its controlling shareholder? 
 
(ii)

value of maintaining a controlling stake in LCC? How does it determine the 
appropriate ownership level, taking into account LCC’s need to maintain

group’s stake to return capital to shareholders or redeploy it elsewhere? 
 
(iii) 
Has the board considered distributing shares of LCC to its own shareholders, 
via a distribution in specie?

On 16 January 2026, SGX RegCo issued a Regulator’s Column on forward guidance, in 
which the regulator strongly encouraged issuers to provide meaningful forward-looking 
disclosures. 
 
SGX RegCo noted that forward-looking information consistently ranks highly among the 
information sought by investors, including institutional investors and research analysts, 
particularly regarding anticipated earnings and management’s strategy for achieving those 
outcomes. The regulator also clarified that forward guidance does not require auditor sign-
off and that issuers are not expected to update guidance immediately for every change in 
circumstances. Issuers should nevertheless make timely announcements in accordance with 
existing listing rules relating to material information and price-sensitive developments. 
 
SGX RegCo also highlighted that forward guidance should be viewed as a means for 
companies to signal confidence, build credibility with investors, and potentially support 
long-term shareholder value, rather than as a compliance exercise. 
 
The Regulator’s Column can be accessed here: 

https://www.sgxgroup.com/media-centre/20260116-regulators-column-forward- 
guidance-why-it-matters-and-how-get-it 
 
(i) 
Can management provide shareholders with greater visibility on the 
group’s current order book? 
 
(ii) 
Given SGX RegCo’s encouragement of forward guidance and its view that 
such disclosures can enhance investor confidence and credibility, has the 
board considered and/or formally evaluated the adoption of a structured 
forward guidance framework for FY26/27 to provide shareholders with 
greater visibility on the group’s outlook, performance, key operating 
assumptions, and strategic priorities? If not, why not?
